facts.statement: Diabloceratops was a medium-sized, quadrupedal herbivore that grew up to 4.5 meters in length and weighed 1.3 metric tons.
facts.quote: Diabloceratops was a medium-sized, moderately built, ground-dwelling, quadrupedal herbivore, that could grow up to an estimated 4.5 m in length and 1.3 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: At the time of its discovery, Diabloceratops was the oldest-known ceratopsid and the first centrosaurine found south of Montana.
facts.quote: At the time of its discovery, it was the oldest-known ceratopsid, and first centrosaurine known from latitudes south of the U.S. state of Montana.

facts.statement: The name Diabloceratops means "devil-horned face", derived from the Spanish word for devil and the Greek term for horned face.
facts.quote: The generic name Diabloceratops means "devil-horned face", coming from Diablo, Spanish for "devil", and ceratops, Latinized Greek for "horned face".

facts.statement: The species Diabloceratops eatoni was named and described in 2010 by James Ian Kirkland and Donald DeBlieux.
facts.quote: The type species, Diabloceratops eatoni, was named and described in 2010 by James Ian Kirkland and Donald DeBlieux.

facts.statement: The only known specimen of Diabloceratops eatoni was found in the Last Chance Creek Member of the Wahweap Formation in Kane County, Utah.
facts.quote: The only specimen of Diabloceratops eatoni was recovered at the Last Chance Creek Member of the Wahweap Formation, in Kane County, Utah.

facts.statement: The type specimen UMNH VP 16699 was collected by Don DeBlieux in 2002 from intraclastic sandstone deposited during the Campanian stage of the Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Type specimen UMNH VP 16699 was collected by Don DeBlieux in 2002, at the Last Chance Creek locality of this formation, in intraclastic sandstone that was deposited during the Campanian stage of the Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: The type specimen consists of a partial skull with part of the lower jaw, where the right side is intact but the left side is weathered.
facts.quote: It consists of a partial skull with a piece of the lower jaw, with the right side being intact and part of the left side, which has been weathered.

facts.statement: A second specimen, UMNH VP 16704, was discovered in 1998 by Joshua A. Smith and assigned to Diabloceratops in 2010.
facts.quote: Another specimen, UMNH VP 16704, was discovered years earlier in 1998 by Joshua A. Smith of the same formation, but was not described until 2010, when it was assigned to Diabloceratops.

facts.statement: Some researchers suggest that specimen UMNH VP 16704 is more similar to Machairoceratops, Yehuecauhceratops, and Menefeeceratops than to Diabloceratops due to the fan-shaped end of the squamosal.
facts.quote: Some researchers suggest that the UMNH VP 16704 specimen is more similar to Machairoceratops, Yehuecauhceratops and Menefeeceratops than to Diabloceratops due to the fan-shaped shape end of the squamosal.

facts.statement: Diabloceratops had a pair of very long spikes on its frill, similar to those found in Einiosaurus and Styracosaurus.
facts.quote: Upon the frill it also had a pair of very long spikes as in Einiosaurus and Styracosaurus.

facts.statement: Diabloceratops possesses an accessory opening in the skull that is reduced or absent in later, more advanced ceratopsids.
facts.quote: Both possess an accessory opening in the skull that would become much reduced or disappear in later, more advanced ceratopsids.

facts.statement: Subsequent phylogenetic analyses continue to classify Diabloceratops as a basal centrosaurine.
facts.quote: Subsequent studies still consider this genus as a basal centrosaurine based on phylogenetic analyses.

facts.statement: The Wahweap Formation, where Diabloceratops fossils were found, has been radiometrically dated between 82.2 and 77.3 million years old.
facts.quote: The Wahweap Formation has been radiometrically dated as being between 82.2 and 77.3 million years old.

facts.statement: During the time Diabloceratops lived, the Western Interior Seaway was at its widest extent, nearly isolating southern Laramidia from the rest of North America.
facts.quote: During the time that Diabloceratops lived, the Western Interior Seaway was at its widest extent, almost completely isolating southern Laramidia from the rest of North America.

facts.statement: The habitat of Diabloceratops included lakes, floodplains, and east-flowing rivers.
facts.quote: The area where dinosaurs lived included lakes, floodplains, and east-flowing rivers.

facts.statement: Evidence suggests that the climate where Diabloceratops lived was wet and seasonal.
facts.quote: The presence of rapid sedimentation and other evidence suggests a wet, seasonal climate.

facts.statement: Diabloceratops shared its environment with hadrosaurs, lambeosaurs, ankylosaurs, pachycephalosaurs, and the theropod Lythronax argestes, likely the apex predator.
facts.quote: Diabloceratops shared its paleoenvironment with other dinosaurs, such as the hadrosaur Acristavus gagslarsoni, and the lambeosaur Adelolophus hutchisoni, unnamed ankylosaurs and pachycephalosaurs, and the theropod Lythronax argestes, which was likely the apex predator in its ecosystem.

facts.statement: The trace fossil includes mammalian den complexes and digging grooves presumably made by a maniraptoran dinosaur.
facts.quote: The trace fossil includes at least two fossilized mammalian den complexes as well as associated digging grooves presumably caused by a maniraptoran dinosaur.

facts.statement: The genus Diabloceratops was established by Kirkland and DeBlieux in 2010.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Kirkland & DeBlieux, 2010

facts.statement: Diabloceratops was a medium-sized, moderately built, ground-dwelling quadrupedal herbivore that could grow up to an estimated 5.5 meters in length.
facts.quote: Diabloceratops era un herbívoro cuadrúpedo terrestre mediano, moderadamente construido, que podría crecer hasta una longitud estimada de 5,5 metros.

facts.statement: Diabloceratops lived at the end of the Cretaceous Period, approximately 79.9 million years ago during the Campanian, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 79,9 millones de años durante el Campaniense, en lo que hoy es Norteamérica.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen UMNH VP 16699 was collected by Don Deblieux in 2002 at the Last Chance Creek locality.

facts.statement: The specific name honors paleontologist Jeffrey Eaton of Weber State University, a friend of the lead author Jim Kirkland.

facts.statement: Diabloceratops is a basal genus within the Centrosaurinae subfamily.

facts.statement: Kirkland noted that Diabloceratops shared characteristics with the more "primitive" Protoceratopsidae.

facts.statement: Both Diabloceratops and Protoceratopsidae possess a supplementary opening in the skull that tends to reduce or disappear in more advanced ceratopsians.
facts.quote: Ambos poseen una abertura suplementaria en el cráneo que tendería a reducirse o desaparecer en los posteriores ceratópsidos más avanzados.

facts.statement: The Wahweap Formation, where Diabloceratops lived, has been radiometrically dated between 81 and 76 million years ago.

facts.statement: The habitat included lakes, floodplains, and rivers flowing eastward.

facts.statement: Rapid sedimentation and other evidence suggest a seasonal humid climate.

facts.statement: Diabloceratops shared its environment with dinosaurs such as the hadrosaurid Acristavus gagslarsoni, the lambeosaurine Adelolophus hutchisoni, unnamed ankylosaurids and pachycephalosaurs, and the apex predator theropod Lythronax argestes.

facts.statement: In 2010, a unique fossil trackway was discovered suggesting a predator-prey relationship between dinosaurs and primitive mammals.
facts.quote: En 2010, se descubrió un rastro fósil único que sugiere una relación depredador-presa entre los dinosaurios y los mamíferos primitivos.

facts.statement: The fossil trackway includes at least two complex fossil mammal burrows and excavation slots supposedly caused by a maniraptoran dinosaur.
facts.quote: El rastro fósil incluye al menos dos complejos fósiles de guaridas de mamíferos, así como ranuras de excavación asociadas supuestamente causadas por un dinosaurio maniraptor.
